exampleAnswers.title: Calculating the Derivative of a Function From Its Graph

question.text: The graph of the function $y = f(x)$ is given above. Find $f'(4).$
question.explanation:
To compute $f'(4),$ we need to find the slope of the tangent to $f(x)$ at $x=4.$

Let's consider the graph of $y=f(x)$ on $[3,5].$ Notice that $x=4$ lies in this interval.

The slope of $y=f(x)$ on $x\in(3,5)$ is constant and equals

\[ \dfrac{\Delta f}{\Delta x} = \dfrac{-3 - 0}{5 -3} = -\dfrac{3}{2}. \]

Therefore, $f'(4)= -\dfrac{3}{2}.$

question.text: The graph of the function $y = f(x)$ is given above. Find $f'(5).$
question.explanation:
To compute $f'(5),$ we need to find the slope of the tangent to $f(x)$ at $x=5.$

Let's consider the graph of $y=f(x)$ for $x\in [4,6].$ Notice that $x=5$ lies in this interval.

The slope of $y=f(x)$ on $x\in(4,6)$ is constant and equals \begin{align*} \dfrac{\Delta f}{\Delta x} &= \dfrac{5-(-1)}{6-4} = \dfrac{6}{2} = 3. \end{align*}

Therefore, $f'(5)= \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{3}.$

question.text: The graphs of the functions $y=f(x)$ and $y=g(x)$ are given above. Find $h'(1)$ where $h(x)= f(x) + g(x).$
question.explanation:
The addition and constant multiple rules for derivatives give \[ h'(x) = f'(x) + g'(x). \]

As a result, we have that \[ h'(1) =f'(1) + g'(1). \]

Also, notice that $x=1$ corresponds to

  • the interval $x\in(-1,2)$ for the function $f,$ and

  • the interval $x\in(-1,2)$ for the function $g,$

as shown below.

  • The slope of $y=f(x)$ is constant on $x\in(-1,2)$ and equals \[ \dfrac{\Delta f}{\Delta x} = \dfrac{1 - (-2)}{2-(-1)} = 1. \] Therefore, $f'(1)=1.$

  • The slope of $y=g(x)$ is constant on $x\in(-1,2)$ and equals \[ \dfrac{\Delta g}{\Delta x} = \dfrac{-2 - 1}{2 - (-1)} = -1. \] Therefore, $g'(1)= -1.$

Finally, we have \begin{align*} h'\left(1\right) &= f'\left( 1 \right) + g'\left( 1 \right) \\[5pt] &= 1 + (-1) \\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{0}. \end{align*}

question.text: The graphs of the functions $y=f(x)$ and $y=g(x)$ are given above. Find $h'(2)$ where $h(x)= g(x)-f(x).$
question.explanation:
The addition and constant multiple rules for derivatives give

\[ h'(x) = g'(x) - f'(x). \]

As a result, we have that

\[ h'(2) =g'(2) - f'(2). \]

Also, notice that $x=2$ corresponds to

  • the interval $x\in(-1,3)$ for the function $f,$ and

  • the interval $x\in(-1,3)$ for the function $g,$

as shown below.

  • The slope of $y=f(x)$ is constant on $x\in(-1,3)$ and equals \[ \dfrac{\Delta f}{\Delta x} = \dfrac{4-1}{3-(-1)} = \dfrac{3}{4}. \] Therefore, $f'(2)=\dfrac{3}{4}.$

  • The slope of $y=g(x)$ is constant on $x\in(-1,3)$ and equals \[ \dfrac{\Delta g}{\Delta x} = \dfrac{1-4}{3-(-1)} =-\dfrac{3}{4}. \] Therefore, $g'(2)=-\dfrac{3}{4}.$

Finally, we have

\begin{align*} h'\left(2\right) &= g'\left(2\right) - f'\left(2\right) \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{3}{4} - \dfrac{3}{4} \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{3}{2}. \end{align*}

question.text: The graphs of the functions $y = f(x)$ and $y=g(x)$ are given above. Find $h'\left(2\right)$ where $h(x)=-2f(x) + 3g(x).$
question.explanation:
The addition and constant multiple rules for derivatives give

\[ h'(x) =-2 f'(x) + 3g'(x). \]

As a result, we have that

\[ h'(2) =-2f'(2) + 3g'(2). \]

Also, notice that $x=2$ corresponds to

  • the interval $x\in(1,3)$ for the function $f,$ and

  • the interval $x\in(1,3)$ for the function $g,$

as shown below.

  • The slope of $y=f(x)$ is constant on $x\in(1,3)$ and equals \[ \dfrac{\Delta f}{\Delta x} = \dfrac{2 - 1}{3-1} = \dfrac{1}{2}. \] Therefore, $f'(2)=\dfrac{1}{2}.$

  • The slope of $y=g(x)$ is constant on $x\in(1,3)$ and equals \[ \dfrac{\Delta g}{\Delta x} = \dfrac{3-(-1)}{3-1} = 2. \] Therefore, $g'(2)=2.$

Finally, we have

\begin{align*} h'\left(2\right) &= -2 f'\left(2\right) + 3g'\left(2\right) \\[5pt] &= (-2)\cdot \dfrac{1}{2} + 3 \cdot 2 \\[5pt] &= 5. \end{align*}

question.text: The graphs of the functions $y=f(x)$ and $y=g(x)$ are given above. Find $h'(3)$ where $h(x)= f(x)-2g(x).$
question.explanation:
The addition and constant multiple rules for derivatives give \[ h'(x) =f'(x) - 2g'(x). \]

As a result, we have that \[ h'(3) =f'(3) - 2g'(3). \]

Also, notice that $x = 3$ corresponds to

  • the interval $x\in(2,4)$ for the function $f,$ and

  • the interval $x\in(0,4)$ for the function $g,$

as shown below.

  • The slope of $y=f(x)$ is constant on $x\in(2,4)$ and equals \[ \dfrac{\Delta f}{\Delta x} = \dfrac{-2-2}{4-2} = -2. \] Therefore, $f'(3)=-2.$

  • The slope of $y=g(x)$ is constant on $x\in(0,4)$ and equals \[ \dfrac{\Delta g}{\Delta x} = \dfrac{-2-0}{4-0} = -\dfrac{1}{2}. \] Therefore, $g'(3)=-\dfrac{1}{2}.$

Finally, we have \begin{align*} h'\left(3\right) &= f'\left(3\right) - 2g'\left(3\right) \\[5pt] &= -2 - 2\cdot \left(-\dfrac{1}{2} \right) \\[5pt] &= -1. \end{align*}

exampleAnswers.title: Computing the Derivative of a Product of Functions

question.text: The graphs of the functions $y=f(x)$ and $y=g(x)$ are given above. Find $h'(-1.5)$ where $h(x)=f(x)g(x).$
question.explanation:
The product rule for derivatives gives

\[ h'(x)=f'(x)\cdot g(x)+f(x)\cdot g'(x). \]

As a result, we have that

\[ h'(-1.5)=f'(-1.5)\cdot g(-1.5)+f(-1.5)\cdot g'(-1.5). \]

From the graphs above, we obtain that $f(-1.5)=-0.5$ and $g(-1.5)=-0.5.$

Additionally:

  • The slope of $f(x)$ on $x\in(-2.5,0)$ equals $1.$ So, $f'(-1.5)=1.$

  • The slope of $g(x)$ on $x\in(-3,-0.5)$ equals $0.$ So, $g'(-1.5)=0.$

Therefore,

\begin{align*} h'(-1.5)&=f'(-1.5)\cdot g(-1.5)+f(-1.5)\cdot g'(-1.5) \\[5pt] &= 1 \cdot (-0.5) + (-0.5) \cdot 0 \\[5pt] &= -0.5. \end{align*}

question.text: The graphs of the functions $y=f(x)$ and $y=g(x)$ are given above. Find $h'(-2)$ where $h(x)=f(x)g(x).$
question.explanation:
The product rule and the addition rule for derivatives give

\[ h'(x) = f'(x)\cdot g(x)+f(x)\cdot g'(x) . \]

As a result, we have that

\[ h'(-2)= f'(-2)\cdot g(-2)+f(-2)\cdot g'(-2) . \]

From the graphs above, we obtain that $f(-2)=0$ and $g(-2)=3.$

Additionally,

  • The slope of $f(x)$ on $x\in(-4,0)$ equals $-1.$ So, $f'(-2)=-1.$

  • The slope of $g(x)$ on $x\in(-4,0)$ equals $\dfrac{1}{2}.$ So, $g'(-2)=\dfrac{1}{2}.$

Therefore,

\begin{align*} h'(-2) &= f'(-2)\cdot g(-2)+f(-2)\cdot g'(-2) - f'(-2) \\[5pt] &=-1 \cdot 3 + 0 \cdot\left( \dfrac{1}{2} \right) \\[5pt] &= -3. \end{align*}

exampleAnswers.title: Computing the Derivative of a Quotient of Functions

question.text: Given the plots of $y=f(x)$ and $y=g(x)$ above, find $h'(-2)$ where $h(x)=\dfrac{f(x)}{g(x)}.$
question.explanation:
The quotient rule for derivatives gives \[ h'(x) = \dfrac{f'(x)\cdot g(x)-f(x)\cdot g'(x)}{(g(x))^2}. \]

As a result, we have that \[ h'(-2) = \dfrac{f'(-2)\cdot g(-2) - f(-2)\cdot g'(-2)}{(g(-2))^2}. \]

From the graphs above, we obtain that $f(-2) = 1$ and $g(-2)=2.$

Additionally:

  • The slope of $f(x)$ on $x \in (-3,-1)$ equals $0.$ So, $f'(-2) = 0.$

  • The slope of $g(x)$ on $x \in (-3,1)$ equals $-1.$ So, $g'(-2)=-1.$

Finally, we have \begin{align*} h'(-2) &= \dfrac{f'(-2)\cdot g(-2) - f(-2)\cdot g'(-2)}{(g(-2))^2} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{0 \cdot 2 - 1 \cdot (-1)}{ (2 )^2} \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{ 1 }{4} \\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac 1 4}. \end{align*}

question.text: Given the plots of $y=f(x)$ and $y=g(x)$ above, find $h'(-2)$ where $h(x)=\dfrac{f(x)}{g(x)}.$
question.explanation:
The quotient rule for derivatives gives \[ h'(x) = \dfrac{f'(x)\cdot g(x)-f(x)\cdot g'(x)}{(g(x))^2}. \]

As a result, we have that \[ h'(-2) = \dfrac{f'(-2)\cdot g(-2) - f(-2)\cdot g'(-2)}{(g(-2))^2}. \]

From the graphs above, we obtain that $f(-2) = 3$ and $g(-2)=2.$

Additionally:

  • The slope of $f(x)$ on $x \in (-3,-1)$ equals $-1.$ So, $f'(-2) = -1.$

  • The slope of $g(x)$ on $x \in (-3,-1)$ equals $-1.$ So, $g'(-2)=-1.$

Finally, we have \begin{align*} h'(-2) &= \dfrac{f'(-2)\cdot g(-2) - f(-2)\cdot g'(-2)}{(g(-2))^2} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{(-1) \cdot 2 - 3 \cdot (-1)}{ (2 )^2} \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{ 1 }{4} \\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac 1 4}. \end{align*}

question.text: Given the plots of $y=f(x)$ and $y=g(x)$ above, find $h'\left(\dfrac{7}{2}\right)$ where $h(x)=\dfrac{f(x)}{g(x)}.$
question.explanation:
The quotient rule for derivatives gives

\[ h'(x) = \dfrac{f'(x)\cdot g(x)-f(x)\cdot g'(x)}{(g(x))^2}. \]

As a result, we have that

\[ h'\left(\dfrac{7}{2}\right) = \dfrac{f'\left(\dfrac{7}{2}\right)\cdot g\left(\dfrac{7}{2}\right)-f\left(\dfrac{7}{2}\right)\cdot g'\left(\dfrac{7}{2}\right)}{\left(g\left(\dfrac{7}{2}\right)\right)^2} \]

From the graph above, we obtain that $f\left(\dfrac{7}{2}\right)=g\left(\dfrac{7}{2}\right)=1.$

Additionally:

  • The slope of $f(x)$ on $x\in(3,4)$ equals $-2.$ So, $f'\left(\dfrac{7}{2}\right)=-2.$

  • The slope of $g(x)$ on $x\in(2,4)$ equals $0.$ So, $g'\left(\dfrac{7}{2}\right)=0.$

Finally, we have

\begin{align*} h'\left(\dfrac{7}{2}\right) &= \dfrac{f'\left(\dfrac{7}{2}\right)g\left(\dfrac{7}{2}\right)-f\left(\dfrac{7}{2}\right)g'\left(\dfrac{7}{2}\right)}{\left(g\left(\dfrac{7}{2}\right)\right)^2} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\left(-2\right) \cdot \left(1\right) - 1 \cdot 0}{1^2} \\[5pt] &= -2. \end{align*}
